articles.text: Despite cold weather on Friday, January 9, Piedmont Unplugged launched its first organized bike bus, drawing up to 50 children ready to ride to Havens Elementary School. The group was assisted by a Piedmont police escort trained in bicycle safety. P i e d m o n t U n p l u g g e d co-founder Danielle Horowitz said she was surprised by the turnout. “To be honest, I thought maybe we’d be lucky if we got 12 people,” she said. Most of the children were five to six years old. While some struggled at the start, their confidence grew as the ride continued. “I think the kids didn’t know they could do it,” Horowitz said. “And once they did it, they felt like rock stars.” The bike bus was created in response to AC Transit’s decision to replace bus line 33 and eliminate extended school-hour service that previously connected the Hampton and Estates Drive area with Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Havens Elementary School. Co-founder Melissa Partovi said the goal of the bike bus is to build a community culture that supports child independence and autonomy. “We want to give kids the confidence to bike to school on their own and parents the fortitude to let this happen,” Partovi said. “The idea is to move toward riding solo, without these guardrails. The flat tax resulted in 76% of Piedmont taxpayers whose parcels are under 10,000 sf paying 6% to 21% more. A small percentage of taxpayers with homes on large parcels and commercial/multi-unit building owners enjoyed tax decreases of 7% to 80%. The school’s pollster Dr. McLarney in 2019 when asked to compare a per square foot of building tax (PSFBT) to a flat rate tax, found 73.5% of voters would support a 125% increased PSFBT. Dr. McLarney found less enthusiasm at 62.1% of voters supporting a 115% increased flat tax. In summary the PSFBT generated 9% more income and 11% more support. Dr. McLarney summarized: “more tax sensitivity for flat tax, less tax sensitivity for square foot version.” The School Board chose to ignore its contracted pollster and put before voters the lower polling regressive flat tax rather than the PSFBT. However, the Board did place a supplemental PSFBT before voters which suggests they recognized two fundamental concepts. First a larger home will cost more initially and will sell for more than a smaller home of equivalent quality. If over a given period of time home prices double, then the $1M home nets $1M profit and the $2M home nets $2M. Secondly a family in a large home will put more children in our schools than a smaller home. In fairness those in larger homes that enjoy greater financially benefit at time of sale and use more school resources should pay a tax based on larger home size. Only a progressive PSFBT brings our tax structure closer to equality for taxpayers of California’s most expensive school support tax, a tax critical to land value in Piedmont. The School Board can now place before voters a progressive tax based on square foot of building. Such a tax makes small incremental increases easy going forward. A PSFBT also attracts young families to the smaller starter homes and encourages increased enrollment. The Alameda School District and others use a PSFBT with a legally allowed lower flat tax on undeveloped parcels and a maximum cap so very large homes are not taxed exorbitantly. The School Board proposes an Evergreen tax which will preclude a tax conversation going forward if passed. This makes a progressive PSFBT critically needed now and for the future of Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council voted Jan. 5 to approve an overall budget and authorize the city administrator to negotiate contract amendments with Hood Design Studio for the Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial Project. The project has a total budget of $417,250. Of that amount, $107,250 is allocated for design and construction-ready drawings. The remaining $250,000 is designated for fabrication of the structure, the foundation, transportation and installation of the artwork. The project is budgeted in the city’s fiscal year 2025–26 budget. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation is partnering with the city on fundraising efforts, with a goal of raising $30,000 for the project. The city is working with renowned artist and landscape architect Walter Hood of Oakland-based Hood Design Studio. Inside, interpretive features will share the Dearings’ story and invite reflection on broader themes of racial exclusion and resilience. This four-year-old tabby is cautious around new people and is looking for a bighearted adopter who will give her the time and trust she needs to blossom into an affectionate companion. Her foster describes her as a “wonderful cat” and says watching her personality unfold is deeply rewarding. She lets you know when she is ready for affection with a gentle nose nudge or by settling into your lap, and prefers soft petting in small doses. Giving her personal space is key to her happiness, but she is not aloof. Talking to her sweetly goes a long way, and she enjoys chatting back. articles.text: The Planning Commission is considering whether to recommend that the City Council adopt proposed “Objective Design Standards” that would govern new housing construction in Piedmont. The proposal updates existing standards for accessory dwelling units, mixed-use projects and multifamily development, and introduces new objective standards for single-family homes and residential projects of up to four units. The draft Objective Design Standards are intended to create clear, measurable and enforceable rules for housing design, giving residents, property owners and developers a better understanding of what new housing in Piedmont is expected to look like. While the standards do not prescribe specific architectural styles, they are designed to produce housing that is consistent with existing development in the city. The draft standards reflect community feedback as well as existing design guidelines. They were informed by two open house events, an online survey and two Planning Commission study sesDraft Objective Design Standards cover page sions. Proposed standards related to driveways and window placement address commonly raised concerns about safety and privacy. State law now requires cities to approve certain types of housing, including accessory dwelling units and SB 9 applications, using “objective” standards that do not rely on subjective judgment by public officials. These state-mandated, ministerial permits do not consider public comment and are not reviewed by the Planning Commission at a public meeting, unlike the traditional design review process. If the Planning Commission votes to recommend the draft Objective Design Standards, the proposal is tentatively scheduled to come before the City Council for adoption in February. Learn more about this initiative and see materials and video from previous discussions at piedmont.ca.gov/ObjectiveDesignStandards.

articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club is inviting residents to a discussion on preparedness titled “Living With Wildfire.” The event is on January 21 at 9:30 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall, and is free to the public The Pacific Palisades fire, which burned in January 2025, served as a reminder that wildfire danger is no longer limited to rural areas. Suburban and urban neighborhoods, including those in the East Bay, face growing risk due to changing climate conditions, dense development, and landscaping choices. The Living With Wildfire program, featuring Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan and photographer Saxon Holt, will present essential practices to help keep your home safe from wildfires and showcase effective fire-wise landscaping techniques you can use. Chief Brannigan will also explain the importance of the recent designation of Piedmont as a Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) and the adoption of the State’s new WUI Fire Code. “Last year’s Palisades Fire was a stark reminder that wildfire isn’t a ‘what if’ — it’s a reality that communities across California need to adapt to, now,” said Brannigan. “The good news is there are practical steps everyone can take today to reduce risk. I’m excited to partner with the Piedmont Garden Club and Saxon Holt to show that outdoor spaces can be both fire-smart and beautiful.” HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: The Grand-Mandana Gas Station is fenced off Several Piedmont-area gas stations have temporarily closed after a long-planned state requirement took effect January 1, mandating the removal or replacement of older single-walled underground fuel tanks that lack modern leak-detection systems. The closures stem from a California law adopted September 25, 2014, which updated the state’s underground storage tank (UST) program governing tank design and construction. The law requires any single-walled storage tank that lacks secondary containment and a continuous leak-detection system to be permanently closed by December 31, 2025. Single-walled storage tanks are considered higher risk because they are more susceptible to leaks caused by rust and corrosion. The intent of the law is to prevent hazardous substances from contaminating soil, groundwater, streams and other sources of drinking water. Owners of single-walled UST systems were notified of the requirement in 2014. As of 2024, Alameda County had 469 gas stations, and five percent, or 23 stations, had not complied with the law ahead of the closure deadline, according to county data. AddiA tank is being delivered to the Grand-Mandana Gas Station tional information is available at https://tinyurl.com/mphd94ad. The State Water Resources Control Board’s UST map identifies Piedmont Gas and Auto Repair, Piedmont Market 76 and the Grand-Mandana gas station as locations required to replace their single-walled tanks. The map can be viewed at https://tinyurl.com/ WaterBoardMapUST. Stations that remain out of compliance face penalties ranging from $500 to $5,000 per day per underground storage tank, according to the State Resources Control Board. Noncompliant stations may also be red-tagged by the Unified Program Agency, which can prevent fuel deliveries and dispensing. To support compliance, California established the Replacing, Removing, or Upgrading Underground Storage Tanks (RUST) program. Since 2015, the State Water Board has provided $183.1 million in loans and grants to assist with the permanent closure of single-walled tanks. Work is already underway at the Grand-Mandana station, where removal and replacement of its single-walled tank began in December. A large excavation is visible at the site where the tank was removed. An employee at Piedmont Gas and Auto Repair told the Post the station expects to remain closed for approximately three months while completing the required work. articles.text: Ruchi Medhekar presided over her first full school board meeting as President on January 7. Since the meeting was held in the Alan Harvey Theater’s drama classroom, she still awaits her first chance to sound the gavel in City Hall to open a meeting from the center chair of the council chamber room. This meeting kicked off new leadership tenures and also served as a farewell and thank you to the fall semester student representatives of the board Hunter Fasteau (PHS) and Saniyah Johnson (MHS). The presentation on the evening was delivered by Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich, focusing the council on their current place in time at the midpoint of the board’s three-year Local Control & Accountability Plan (LCAP). “It’s really hard to believe we are in year two of our three-year LCAP, halfway through. I’m such a huge fan of everything we have done this year from Fish Tank to the World Language update,” said Medhekar. Medhekar’s vice president title was filled by second year board member Michael Malione who will also serve an important leadership role on the board this calendar year. As president, Medhekar introduced her first new resolution for the board, a first reading seeking to renewing the Measure G school parcel tax for $3174 per parcel. Medhekar thanked board members Max Roman and Lindsay Thomasson for putting a special tax on the ballot, “It’s not something that any of us take lightly, so thank you for that,” Medhekar said. Piedmont resident Rick Schiller spoke in the public comment portion of the meeting promoting a shift of the financial burden to the square foot tax. He suggested large homes use more school resources and should pay more accordingly. “Only a progressive per square foot of building tax makes equality and fairness possible,” said Schiller. Schiller went over his allotted time, requiring new president Medhekar, for the first time, to inform a speaker that their time was up. Mehhekar handled this delicate responsibility with grace, affecting the appropriate concern and care with her words and tone. A significant part of the role is being the public facing voice for the board, and encounters with public speakers will provide a continual test of empathy. Medhekar’s first meeting as president took place on the first day back from school, beginning a new spring semester for students. The meeting was relatively short, lasting only one hour. The newly reorganized board will next meet on Wednesday, January 21, which will include Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s State of the District report.

articles.text: At the beginning of a new year, we often ask big questions: What do I want to change? What do I want to make? What do I want to become better at? They are reasonable questions. They can also be completely paralyzing, because they are so big. Creativity often stalls not because people lack ideas, but because the imagined next step feels too large or too loaded with expectation. We leap immediately to outcomes like mastery, consistency or meaning before giving ourselves permission to simply begin. I’ve been wondering what might happen if we made the entry point much smaller, maybe even just one thing. Not “what should I commit my entire being to this year,” but a simple experiment: • A new walking route. • A different genre of book. • Learning to cook a new recipe. • Saying yes to an invitation you would normally decline. • Moving one idea from germ to first step. When the stakes are low, something interesting can happen. Curiosity has room to breathe. Attention sharpens because you are no longer trying to prove anything. You are simply gathering information. This is how creativity often works. Not in sweeping gestures or giant leaps, but in small acts of willingness, a quiet openness to what might happen if you do something slightly different than yesterday. What I like about starting here is that it does not require confidence, talent or clarity about where things are headed. It only requires noticing a flicker of interest and being willing to follow it. You might try this experiment for the next week or month: when something catches your attention, try it, even once. Do not worry about whether it is useful or impressive. In fact, aim for the novel. Not everything you try will lead somewhere, and that is not the point. The point is to remind yourself that creativity does not begin with certainty. It begins with small movements. One small step is often enough to change the energy of an entire year. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/

articles.text: the return to school. As we enter the spring season, the Piedmont Unified School District is preparing for upcoming negotiations with our employee associations. We are writing to share the Board’s priorities and reaffirm our appreciation for our educators and staff who serve our students each day. Perhaps most important, we want to be clear that we view our staff as the heart of our schools. Their expertise, care, and dedication create the learning environments that allow our students to thrive academically and socially. The Board is committed to supporting their professional success and well-being. As we approach negotiations, the Board has identified several key priorities that reflect our shared values and our long-term responsibility to students, staff, and our community. Ensuring Competitive and Sustainable Compensation Attracting and retaining outstanding educators and staff require a salary structure that is competitive within our region. We continue to review comparable school districts and believe that improving the salaries of our newest teachers must be a priority for our district in order to attract and retain beginning teachers. We are pleased with our progress in raising veteran teacher pay, but our work is not finished. We are now focused on increasing starting salaries to ensure we attract the best new educators. Investing in our beginning teachers is an investment in a stable, high-quality workforce for the future. Providing Affordable and High-Quality Healthcare The Board recognizes that access to affordable healthcare is a critical component of employee wellbeing. Two years ago, rising healthcare costs posed significant challenges for the District. Through thoughtful research, improved $0 cost and multiple low-cost options were identified this year, offering better access to healthcare for employees and their families. Maintaining fiscally responsible, high-quality healthcare options for our staff remains a priority for our District. Protecting the District’s LongTerm Fiscal Health The Board prioritizes longterm fiscal stability to protect our staff and students from economic uncertainty. By maintaining a healthy reserve, the District can manage rising costs and enrollment shifts without compromising class sizes or staffing levels. This responsible management ensures we can provide competitive compensation while maintaining a stable environment for the entire school community. Maintaining Low Class Sizes Small class sizes, particularly in our elementary schools, are foundational to high quality teaching and learning. Low class size allows educators to know students well, personalize instruction, and provide the academic and social emotional support young learners need. We are also analyzing middle and high school class sizes to ensure they remain balanced and low. Earlier this fall, the District held a Board workshop and provided direction for staff to continue to prioritize small class sizes in our core classes in the master schedule in an effort to balance classes. Preserving low class sizes remains a central priority for the Board alongside maintaining flexibility to ensure financial viability for all the priorities articulated above. Sincerely, Ruchi Medhekar, Board President Michael Malione, Vice President Max Roman, Member Susy Struble, Member Lindsay Thomasson, Member Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D., Superintendent

As we enter the spring season, the Piedmont Unified School District is preparing for upcoming negotiations with our employee associations. We are writing to share the Board’s priorities and reaffirm our appreciation for our educators and staff who serve our students each day. Perhaps most important, we want to be clear that we view our staff as the heart of our schools. Their expertise, care, and dedication create the learning environments that allow our students to thrive academically and socially. The Board is committed to supporting their professional success and well-being. As we approach negotiations, the Board has identified several key priorities that reflect our shared values and our long-term responsibility to students, staff, and our community. Ensuring Competitive and Sustainable Compensation Attracting and retaining outstanding educators and staff require a salary structure that is competitive within our region. We continue to review comparable school districts and believe that improving the salaries of our newest teachers must be a priority for our district in order to attract and retain beginning teachers. We are pleased with our progress in raising veteran teacher pay, but our work is not finished. We are now focused on increasing starting salaries to ensure we attract the best new educators. Investing in our beginning teachers is an investment in a stable, high-quality workforce for the future. Providing Affordable and High-Quality Healthcare The Board recognizes that access to affordable healthcare is a critical component of employee wellbeing. Two years ago, rising healthcare costs posed significant challenges for the District. Through thoughtful research, improved $0 cost and multiple low-cost options were identified this year, offering better access to healthcare for employees and their families. Maintaining fiscally responsible, high-quality healthcare options for our staff remains a priority for our District. Protecting the District’s LongTerm Fiscal Health The Board prioritizes longterm fiscal stability to protect our staff and students from economic uncertainty. By maintaining a healthy reserve, the District can manage rising costs and enrollment shifts without compromising class sizes or staffing levels. This responsible management ensures we can provide competitive compensation while maintaining a stable environment for the entire school community. Maintaining Low Class Sizes Small class sizes, particularly in our elementary schools, are foundational to high quality teaching and learning. Low class size allows educators to know students well, personalize instruction, and provide the academic and social emotional support young learners need. We are also analyzing middle and high school class sizes to ensure they remain balanced and low. Earlier this fall, the District held a Board workshop and provided direction for staff to continue to prioritize small class sizes in our core classes in the master schedule in an effort to balance classes. Preserving low class sizes remains a central priority for the Board alongside maintaining flexibility to ensure financial viability for all the priorities articulated above. articles.text: Student representatives on the Piedmont Unified School District Board of Education occupy a distinct role – balancing life as students while representing thousands of peers in district decision-making. The second semester at Piedmont High marks a transition from outgoing student board members Hunter Fasteau and Saniyah Johnson to incoming representatives Charli Panico and Ben Ramakrishnan, highlighting both the promise and limits of student voice in district governance. As Panico begins her term, she is motivated by a desire to move student concerns beyond informal conversations and into action. “I saw an opportunity to speak for my peers,” she said. “This role allows me to turn concerns into actions and make sure student experiences are truly represented.” Ahead of her first board meeting, Panico has focused on gathering perspectives from students across campus on two major issues: the district’s cell phone policy and the introduction of new courses. Rather than assuming a single viewpoint, she has sought out a range of perspectives. “I’ve been going around and talking to people at school and writing down what people need,” she said. Panico has been encouraged by the board’s use of smaller, topic-based meetings and is interested in expanding them at PHS as a way to lower barriers to student participation and connect students directly with board members. While the current pilot limiting phone use during brunch and passing periods has had little impact so far, she expressed concerns about a full ban next year, citing enforcement challenges, safety issues, and accessibility for students with medical needs. She also views new course offerings as an opportunity, but noted that the expansion of weighted classes may increase academic stress. That belief is echoed, albeit more cautiously, by Fasteau, who completed his term last semester. Like Panico, Fasteau ran to represent student perspectives and influence policy, but quickly realized how demanding the role could be. “I wasn’t able to separate this role at all from my life as a student,” he said. One moment that stood out was staying late to cast a vote on the second reading of PHS course additions. “It was about fulfilling the promise I made to the students that informed my decision,” he said. While Fasteau believes board members care about student input, he identified structural challenges that limit consistent representation. He noted that student voice often depends on a single individual and suggested more permanent systems for student feedback. After learning about the Brown Act, which restricts discussion of non-agendized items, he said he sometimes felt “more like an extension of a system as opposed to the voice of the student body.” Despite these limitations, Fasteau emphasized the power of participation. “Students and other adults should know that their voice matters,” he said. “They can influence policy just by showing up.” At the January 7 board meeting, the final meeting for Fasteau and Johnson as student board representatives, Superintendent Hawn publicly thanked both students for their dedication and advocacy. Board President Ruchi Medhekar also addressed the representatives directly, emphasizing the lasting impact of their work. “Every student board member has an opportunity to leave their mark,” Medhekar said. Reflecting on their terms, she expressed gratitude for the ways both students shaped board discussions. She recalled first meeting Fasteau early in his time at PHS and recognizing his deep care for the district, noting that it made him a strong candidate for the role. She also highlighted Johnson’s influence on board decision-making, adding that there are “only a handful of times” when a student is able to meaningfully shift the direction of a resolution, and credited Johnson with changing the board’s perspective on NCAA-related issues. Together, Panico’s forward-looking approach and Fasteau’s reflections illustrate the realities of student representation in Piedmont, defined by opportunity, responsibility, and institutional constraints. As Panico begins her term alongside Ramakrishnan, representing both Piedmont High School and Millennium High School, her leadership builds on lessons from those who came before her. Ultimately, the strength of student voice depends not only on who holds the seat, but on how consistently students are invited and supported to participate. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern reporter for the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Piedmont Cub Scouts in Packs 3, 4, 5 and 6 joined together to help unhoused neighbors by assembling hygiene kits and donating them to the East Oakland Collective. On December 10 more than 80 people, including Cub Scouts (Kinder-5th grade) with their families, adult Cub Scout leaders, Den Chiefs and Scouts helped assemble over 600 hygiene kits at Havens Elementary School. Pack 3 started this annual holiday tradition of assembling hygiene kits in 2023 by donating 300 hygiene kits to East Oakland Collective. Now in its third year, the event has expanded to include all four Piedmont Cub Scout Packs and has more than doubled its giving. This community service project is supported by the four Packs as well as individual Scout families. The hygiene kits included toiletries such as soap, toothbrushes, toothpaste, toilet paper, washcloths, and winter hats. The Programs Manager at the East Oakland Collective said, “We are beyond thankful for the continuous support and generosity of … [Piedmont Cub Scouts]. Their commitment to service and care for our community makes a meaningful impact, and the hygiene kits assembled by the Cub Scouts are a powerful example of how young leaders can truly make a difference.” If you are interested in joining Cub Scouts or Scouts, contact the Piedmont Scout Council at contact@piedmontbsa.org. The East Bay Collective is a non-profit organization that helps East Oakland residents live comfortably in their neighborhoods. One of their biggest events, hosted quarterly, is Feed the Hood, where they distribute food and hygiene kits to the unhoused. If you want to support the East Oakland Collective, please visit eastoaklandcollective.com Cub Scouts, their families, and Scout Leaders

articles.text: It’s been a strong start to the New Year for Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team, tying Western Alameda County Conference rivals Berkeley 2-2 on Thursday, January 8 at the Yellowjackets’ home field, and thrashing Gateway 11-0 at Witter two days later. The results push Piedmont’s unbeaten run to five games with four wins and one draw. “We’re starting to play the kind of football we want to see. The press was really good against Berkeley, they are a very good team. We played well against Berkeley, we moved the ball well, but there’s still things we want to work on as a team,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. The result against Berkeley was Piedmont’s first league match of the season, giving them an important point against a school with 19 upperclassmen. “Our press was outstanding. They struggled to get out of their own half,” Spencer-Harty said. “Berkeley was definitely a hard game. We didn’t know what to expect, but a tie is good for what we got. We’re still figuring out how to work together, plus a new coach is a change. It’s just nice to be back and play,” senior Miranda Liu added. Piedmont’s record is now 4-2-2 (W-T-L) under first-year head coach Spencer-Harty, who came to the Highlanders as another product of the coaching tree produced by the 24-7 UK Soccer Academy. Former girls’ soccer coach Dan Chubbock and former boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan also came from 24-7, as does current boys soccer head coach Ben Russell. “It’s great. I feel like all the 24-7 coaches have a similar vibe, so it doesn’t feel much different. The teams doing great working together, and having four freshmen [Olivia Nealon, Makenna Piedmont is 4-2-2 and on a five-game unbeaten run. Staff Photos Small, Olivia Kan-Miller, Olivia Luccacini] is a big change, but they are great,” Liu said. The Highlanders look ahead to its league schedule ramping up with critical matches against Castro Valley, Alameda, and Bishop O’Dowd ahead. Spencer-Harty likes what he sees out of the group, but still has things he wants to work on. “There’s a little work to be done in our combination play and getting our wingbacks a little higher a little earlier. A lot of time we isolate our two nines, so we want to get support 4-v-3 instead of a 3-v-2 against us,” Spencer-Harty said. 11-0 over Gateway The shellacking started in the third minute following a corner, where Erica Smith turned in a loose ball in front of the net. Seven minutes later, Liu scored on a rebounded initial shot by Ayla Blanford in the box. Liu scored again two minutes later, making a run in behind to put herself 1-on-1 with the goalkeeper. Blanford scored in the 17th after Elia Kwong’s shot on target rebounded into play. Elspeth Grippando made it 5-nil in the 25th in another 1-on- 1. Kwong scored in the 35th, holding off a defender in a long run in possession—bringing it to 6-0 by halftime. Olivia Luccacini scored in the 49th on a nice run down the right side. Grippando scored again in the 51st on a dribble down the left. Lila Rosen scored on a composed shot in the box in the 55th, while freshman Olivia Nealon scored five minutes later. Piedmont’s last goal came by Makenna Small in the 69th minute. 2-2 with Berkeley Berkeley took an initial lead in the 10th minute on a looping header from a corner. Piedmont equalized in the early minutes of the second half when Kwong slotted in a penalty kick off the underside of the crossbar. It came after Liu drew a penalty, weaving her way around three defenders before being pulled down in the box. Berkeley went ahead again a few minutes later when a well struck free-kick rocketed into the top side of the net, giving the Jackets a 2-1 lead. Piedmont started to connect passes, leading to Liu scoring the equalizer in the 60th minute. Liu found a little space on the right side of the box, lofting an inch-perfect shot over the keeper. articles.text: Staff Photos P.J. Brayer scored a career high 27 points in Piedmont’s win over St. Joseph. He also logged 19 points in victory over San Leandro. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team is on a hot streak, with a winning streak now at six games with a pair of victories over the last week on the road. The Highlanders recently beat St. Joseph 69-58 on Saturday, January 10, while they bashed San Leandro 73-49 two days earlier for their first Western Alameda County Conference game of the season. “It feels great, it’s the most wins we’ve had in a row since 2024. Top to bottom, we’re playing really well defensively. I’m proud of the way the guys are competing,” coach Ben Spencer said. Piedmont’s lineup continues to be bolstered by its “Big Three” of upperclassmen, seniors Dillon Casey and P.J. Brayer, and junior Beach Lorin. The trio combined for 116 points over the two games. “They are tough to guard. Dillon is probably going to get the best defender on the other team, Beach will get their second defender, and P.J. is a really tough matchup because he can stretch the floor. A lot of bigs have a hard time guarding P.J. and it just opens things up,” Spencer said. “It’s not just us three, we have guys coming off the bench that I can trust just as much as I can trust the starters. We’re deep this year. Dillon and Beach are helluva players. I just try my best to do my job. I don’t try to do too much, just do my role, and play the best defense I can, get every rebound, and knock down open shots,” Brayer mentioned. Brayer scored a career-high 27 points in their win over St. Joseph. He’s a three-year varsity player, emerging as a marquee scorer and a major presence on the boards. “I think my game is at its peak right now. I’ve put in a lot of work and it’s starting to pay off. The competition in practice has only made me better,” Brayer said. 69-58 victory over St. Joseph Piedmont led 18-15 through the first quarter and extended the score to 26-19 in a low-scoring second quarter. PHS then more than doubled their points total in the third quarter, exploding for 31 points while allowing 17 to build a 57-36 lead. St. Joe finished with 22 points in the fourth, while PHS put up 12 toward the 69-58 final score. Brayer scored 16 of his 27 points in the third quarter, when he knocked down three 3-pointers. Final stats: Brayer led with 27 points, Casey had 20, Lorin had 11, Lucian Fang-Ring scored seven, while Akash Bornstein and Nick Riordan had two. 73-49 over San Leandro San Leandro opened with a 7-4 advantage in the early minutes, but Piedmont took an 8-7 lead with 3:52 left in the opening quarter when Lorin landed a layup. The Highlanders never trailed, puting up another 14 points while allowing four to lead 22-11 by the end of the first quarter. PHS made things comfortable in the second quarter, adding 17 points to the tally to establish a 17-point lead by halftime, up 39-22. The Highlanders added 16 more points in the third while only conceding eight points to Dillon Casey had 22 points against San Leandro and 20 points in a game with St. Joseph.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team split its last two matches, beating Encinal 2-1 on Friday, January 9 in Alameda and losing 3-0 to non-conference Chico two days earlier at Witter Field. The results bring Piedmont’s record to 2-0-6 (W-T-L) to start the new year, which is shaping up to be a season of transition for the defending Division 5 CIF NorCal champions. “We’ve had a lack of ability to execute in overload situations; just poor execution and decision-making. Defensively, we need awareness to manage space and runners,” said coach Ben Russell. Piedmont has shown flashes of its potential and creating chances, but has lacked the finishing touch. Russell said growing pains were expected with a young roster that includes three freshmen, 10 sophomores, five juniors and five seniors, though there are signs of progress. “Individual brilliance is great, but there are basics you have to execute every single day. That’s the habit piece we are preaching. You have to do the basics really well, like connecting the right pass, making sure your touch is good and not allowing attacks to die,” Russell said. Now approaching the midway point of the season, Russell is hopeful Piedmont can mirror last year’s second-half turnaround. The 2024 team finished the early portion of its schedule 2-2-4 before improving during its NCS and CIF runs. “We have to pick up the habit. That’s my big philosophy: intention, behavior, habit. articles.text: In August last fall, PHS Class of 2020 and St. Mary’s College 2025 graduate Luke Barrett signed a contract to play for AMW Arka Gdynia of Poland — joining the professional ranks in European basketball. So far this season, Arka Gdynia is in second-place of the Polish Basketball League with an 11-4 record midway through its 30-game season. Barrett has appeared in all 15 games as a rookie. He is averaging 19.7 minutes per game, converting 67.3 percent of his field goals, 45 percent of 3-pointers, and 81.8 percent of his free throws for 111 points. He’s averaging 5.4 rebounds per game, which is third on the team. “The type of basketball I want to play and type of places that I fit, I knew that from the start. This is a lot closer (in style) to college than the NBA. It is a lot more tactical. It is faster out here than college because of the 24-second shot clock. Here you have guys who have different skillsets. We run the same exact defense we ran in college,” Barrett said, via the Mercury News. Gdynia is a city on the Baltic coast of northern Poland, resting along the Gulf of Gdansk with a population of 257,000. Arka is a nine-time championship winning team and have had several former players appear in the NBA. Barrett joined the team on a one-month trial before landing his first full-time professional contract after finishing his collegiate career at St. Mary’s as a leader. Barrett called the time before landing a deal an excruciating “waiting game.” “Obviously I knew the goal was to get somewhere and play overseas, to play pro and keep playing basketball somewhere. As soon as the season was over, I tried to get an agent. I ended up with an agent that represented three or four of my former college teammates. Those three months (this summer) were tough; it was a waiting game. For me, it took a while to hear anything concrete. articles.text: The rains from recent weeks have tapered off but the results can still be seen in flowing gulches, streams, and creeks. Winter hiking is the best time to visit the local waterfalls, and the Post has ventured to several around the Bay Area. Here’s a collection of local waterfalls to try. Uvas Canyon’s Waterfalls Loop Trail, Morgan Hill In Morgan Hill’s Uvas Canyon County Park are a collection of five accessible waterfalls in 5.2 miles of total hiking. You’ll still require 1,273 feet in elevation gain to see all five in the entire loop—but four of those waterfalls within the first 1.6 miles—making the last long trip to Triple Falls, and optional excursion if you’re worried about tired legs. Cataract Creek, Mt. Tamalpais Watershed The Cataract Falls Trail in the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed is a 4.8 out-and-back with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain. There are two trailheads, parking on Bolinas Fairfax Road will provide just a 0.5 walk to the first waterfall and another 0.2 to its most famous Helen Markt Falls. Should you walk the entire Cataract Falls Trail, you will encounter cascades along cataract creek. Murietta Falls, Del Valle Regional Wilderness Murietta Falls in Livermore’s Del Valle Regional Park is considered the highest waterfall in the entire Bay Area at an elevation of near 3,000 feet in the Ohlone Wilderness, where a small stream cascades over 100 foot cliff-face—meaning this location should only be taken by experienced hikers looking for a challenge. The entire day required 12.1 miles of hiking and near 5,000 feet in elevation gain; it is considered a good training spot for those interested in Half Dome. Alamere Falls, Bolinas The trek to Alamere Falls is a total of 13.6 miles and an elevation gain of 1,811 feet taking Uvas Canyon County Park has five accessible waterfalls to enjoy, including four in the first 1.5 miles

articles.text: Left Coast Chamber Ensemble Left Coast Chamber Ensemble will present Metamorphosen, a chamber music program centered on themes of transformation and reflection, with performances January 31 in Berkeley and February 1 in San Francisco. The concert’s centerpiece is Richard Strauss’ Metamorphosen, or “Transformations,” one of the composer’s most intimate works which provides a resonating response to the devastation of World War II. The piece was composed in 1945 originally written for 23 solo strings. Metamorphosen will be performed in an intimate arrangement by Rudolf Leopold of the Vienna Philharmonic. “Composed in 1945, Strauss’s Metamorphosen is at once a memorial and a transformation,” said LCCE Artistic Director Matilda Hofman in a press release. She described the work as “a hauntingly nostalgic eulogy for a world which was falling apart before his very eyes, while at the same time inspired by the idea that all life, even as it changes and varies, is fundamentally connected.” The program also includes works by Luciano Berio, Robert Hughes and local composer Hendel Almétus, each selected for its ability to draw expressive power from small instrumental forces. Almét us’ Tounen (“To Return”) for solo flute reflects a personal transformation rooted in a deliberate return to his Haitian heritage and cultural values, and invites listeners to dwell within its inner world,” Almétus said, “where unity, balance, and wholeness emerge from diversity — a musical reflection of the perfect place I seek to paint through sound.” The concert will be performed at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, Jan. 31, at the First Church of Christ, Scientist, 2619 Dwight Way, Berkeley, and at 4 p.m. Sunday, Feb. 1, at Noe Valley Ministry, 1021 Sanchez St., San Francisco. Tickets purchased at the door are $43 for general admission and $18 for students. Advance tickets are available for $40 general admission and $15 for students. Visit https://www.leftcoastensemble.org/ for more information. articles.text: Concert held at First Congregational Church of Berkeley Jan. 25 Berkeley Symphony closes its 2025–26 Symphonic Series with Fables & Folklore, a program centered on storytelling and cultural tradition, on Sunday, January 25 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The concert begins at 4 p.m., marking the fourth and final performance of the Symphony’s 54th season series. Internationally acclaimed conductor Carolyn Kuan, music director of the Hartford Symphony Orchestra, will lead the program. “This program celebrates imagination and heritage, honoring cultural roots while inviting audiences to experience the power of storytelling through music,” said Executive Director Marion Atherton in a statement. The evening opens with Folk Songs for Orchestra by composer Huang Ruo. The work draws on traditional Chinese folk melodies, blending them with contemporary orchestral textures to evoke both personal memory and shared cultural history. Guitarist Marc Teicholz will then join the Symphony for O Saci-Pererê, a guitar concerto by composer Clarice Assad inspired by Brazilian folklore. The piece centers on Saci, a mischievous trickster figure from Indigenous and Afro-Brazilian mythology, and features rhythmic energy and playful character alongside deeper reflections on Brazilian identity and oral tradition. Following intermission, the program concludes with Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, a work rooted in the folk music of the Czech countryside. Known for its melodic richness and pastoral warmth, the symphony’s triumphant finale provides a celebratory close to the series. Single tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510-841- 2800. All Symphonic Series concerts take place at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The Berkeley Symphony ends its 54th symphonic season next week.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony ends 54th season with Fables & Folklore

articles.text: Monty Python’s Tony Award– win ning musical comedy SPAMALOT will play a limited engagement at San Francisco’s Golden Gate Theatre from March 3 through March 22. The production is part of the show’s North American tour following a critically acclaimed Broadway revival in 2023. First premiering on Broadway in 2005, SPAMALOT features a book and lyrics by Eric Idle, with music by John Du Prez and Idle. The original production received 14 Tony Award nominations and won three, including Best Musical. The current touring production is directed and choreographed by Josh Rhodes and has been praised for its inventive staging, design, and performances. The cast includes Major Attaway as King Arthur, Sean Bell as Sir Robin, Chris Collins-Pisano as Sir Lancelot, Ellis C. Dawson III as Sir Bedevere, Leo Roberts as Sir Galahad, and Amanda Robles as the Lady of the Lake. Steven Telsey appears as the Historian and Prince Herbert. Adapted from the film Monty Python and the Holy Grail, the musical features well-known songs such as “Always Look on the Bright Side of Life,” “The Song That Goes Like This,” and “Find Your Grail.” Single tickets are on sale now through BroadwaySF. Group sales are also available. Visit www.broadwaysf.com to purchase tickets. Monty Python’s SPAMALOT performed in Washington, D.C.

articles.text: Festival runs Jan. 21 - 25 The FOG Design+Art fair returns to San Francisco’s Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture next week, featuring artwork from more than 60 leading galleries from the Bay Area and around the world. Now in its 14th year, the showcase highlights contemporary art and design through gallery presentations and special installations. The 2026 fair will include both new and returning exhibitors, along with the largest presentation to date of FOG FOCUS, a platform highlighting artists in the earlier stages of their careers. The fair opens on January 21 with a preview gala benefiting the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) education initiatives. “This year’s exhibitors embody the spirit of curiosity and collaboration that makes FOG such a vital part of the Bay Area’s cultural community,” said Sydney Blumenkranz, director of FOG Design+Art, in a press statement. Sixteen galleries will participate in the fair for the first time, including David Nolan Gallery, Goodman, Josh Lilley and Vielmetter in Pier 3, as well as Anat Ebgi, Charlie James Gallery and re.riddle in FOG FOCUS. More than 20 international galleries are expected, representing cities such as London, Paris, Mexico City, São Paulo and Kyoto. Fifteen Bay Area galleries will also take part. FOG FOCUS will feature 16 galleries and offer works at more accessible price points. The fair will also mark the return of FOG MRKT, an entryway installation highlighting artists, designers and makers through editioned and singular works. The showcase also includes FOG Talks, a series of conversations exploring art, design, technology and culture, curated by Susan Swig and included with admission. FOG is open Thursday, January 22 through Saturday, January 24 from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., and Sunday, January 25 from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. A preview gala is held Wednesday, January 21. articles.text: January 17 – February 28 Society of Printmakers’ Art Exhibition The California Society of Printmakers returns to Piedmont with its 111th Annual Members’ Exhibition, showing close to 100 works of printmaking art, demonstrating the incredible variety of style and process that falls within this field. The exhibit will be open on Saturdays and Sundays January 17, 18, 25, and 31, and most February weekends, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.; there will be an opening reception on Saturday, January 24, from 1 to 4 p.m., as well as a closing reception on February 28 from 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., providing good chances of meeting and learning from many of the artists, one or two of whom will also be present during the weekend open hours. The exhibition is free to visit, and the works will also be available to enjoy during your attendance at any of PCA’s public events. Saturday, January 17, 5:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art History Lecture The Impressionist movement is regarded by many as the most important revolution in Western art since the Renaissance. When the Impressionist renegades gathered in 1874 to hold their very first group exhibition outside the state-regulated parameters, many thought they were building the next revolution to upend Paris. In light of the challenges these artists were facing, they relied heavily on their relationships with each other. The most compelling of these relationships was between Berthe Morisot and Édouard Manet. Join local art historian Michael Stehr as he presents a 50-minute illustrated lecture at PCA that celebrates the fascinating relationship between these two titans of the Impressionist movement. The lecture is designed to prepare attendees for the exhibit currently running at the Legion of Honor until March 1, entitled Manet et Morisot. Admission to the lecture is $20 per person, Cash only, at the door. For more info, email Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Saturday, January 31, 7:00 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro Solo Piano Concert The incomparable Italian pianist Cristiana Pegoraro returns to Piedmont for another recital. As president of Narnia Arts Academy and Artistic Director of the Narnia Festival, she has been hailed by the New York Times as “an artist of the highest caliber.” She has performed on the world’s most prestigious stages, including Lincoln Center, Carnegie Hall, the United Nations (New York), the Sydney Opera House, Festspielhaus (Salzburg), Musikverein (Vienna), Royal College of Music (London), Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome), Teatro alla Scala (Milan). She brings to Piedmont a program she premiered in November at Carnegie Hall, called Harmonies of Peace. Advance tickets are available at: https://events. com/r/tickets/1023245. Tickets at the door are $40/adult and $20/youth. Sunday, February 8, 4:00 p.m. Carl Blake / Will Underwood Piano & Flute Duo William Underwood III holds a B.S. in Music from Florida A&M and a Master of Music in Flute Performance from Wayne State. He has toured extensively in Japan with Kyodo Tokyo and regularly works as a soloist, collaborator, and recording artist. Dr. Carl Blake, a local piano master who has performed worldwide to acclaim, has introduced Will to the best of the Bay Area, often playing together as a duo exploring piano and flute repertoire. Tickets and more info will be available soon. Thursday, February 12, 6:30 p.m. Sacha Grippando Jewelry Arts Lecture Throughout history, jewelry and watches have played a vital role in the visual arts, imbuing the wearer with power, wealth, and status. From ancient times, the inclusion of jewels, and later watches, in portraits of royalty and significant figures served to highlight their importance. This illuminating and sparkling lecture will explore how the visual arts utilize jewelry and watches to define characters and convey specific traits. Sacha Grippando will analyze significant works of art, ranging from paintings by masters like Leonardo Da Vinci and Vermeer to modern and contemporary artists like Salvador Dali and Kehinde Wiley. Admission is by $20 suggested donation at the door and includes light refreshments afterwards.

articles.text: Brown Gables, the Alexander home at Sea View and Hampton, was named for its prominent gables, painted brown. Their grand three-story mansion was completed in 1909, which they named “Brown Gables” for its massive gabled dormers with bargeboards, painted brown. The first floor was faced in brick and half timbering covered the upper stories. Two large porte cocheres were also trimmed in brown gables. Diamond-paned, leaded glass windows graced the entry and large bay windows offered expansive views from every room in this most elegant early home in Piedmont. City records indicate that the Alexander house had three living rooms, five bedrooms and five bathrooms. Koa wood and other exotic woods enhanced the interior. It was an exceptional house in 1909 with 3240 square feet and was the site of many festive balls. The gardens of the Alexander home also hosted many garden parties that benefited local charities. Mary Alexander was a strong supporter of the Ladies Relief Society, the Matilda Brown Home and the Women’s Guild of the Piedmont Church. She also organized the Bay Area chapter of the Red Cross at the onset of World War I and led it for over 30 years. Their beautiful gardens extended over nine of today’s lots on Sea View and King Avenues. A low brick wall with a subtle detail surrounded the property. The wall is visible in the photo of the house and portions still stand today on Hampton. The Alexander carriage house, which still exists at 84 King, had servants’ quarters and an indoor swimming pool. Helen Wills Moody, the Wimbledon tennis star in the 1920s and 1930s, practiced on the tennis court there. The Alexander family formed a small community near Sea View and Hampton. In 1911, Wallace’s mother built her own home across the street at 92 Sea View — designed by Charles W. Dickey — and Mary’s mother built her home down the street at 236 Sea View. Wallace Alexander was president of the Alexander and Baldwin sugar firm, Vice President of the Matson Navigation Company, director of several other Hawaiian companies and a trustee of Stanford University. Although he was active in many businesses, he found time for many civic and charitable organizations in Piedmont. In addition to constructing the stores and saving Piedmont Park, Alexander was also the driving force behind the construction of the Piedmont Interdenominational Church (now Piedmont Community Church), arranging for the purchase of the land and again hiring Albert Farr to design the church. Wallace Alexander also established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council. He arranged for the scouts to meet in the basement of the church, as they still do today. In 1929, he leased land from the Forest Service near Keddie in Plumas County and established Camp Wallace Alexander, a Piedmont scouting tradition fondly remembered by generations of Piedmont Boy Scouts. The land lease expired in 1982 and Camp Wallace Alexander was dismantled. In 1939, Wallace Alexander suffered a fatal stroke at his second home in Honolulu. He was eulogized as “Piedmont’s leading private citizen.” Wallace left a large bequest to the Piedmont Community Church and to the Piedmont Boy Scouts. His philosophy was that he “was but a trustee of the money that came to him.” Upon his death, Mary Alexander followed her husband’s wishes that the property be subdivided into 13 lots. Poor eyesight initially kept McNamara from military service during World War II, but he volunteered to train Air Force staff and served in the United States Army Air Forces from 1943 to 1946. He played a key role in the Office of Statistical Control, applying statistical analysis to improve bombing mission planning and logistics. After the war, McNamara joined a team of former military colleagues offering management expertise to companies. Hired by Henry Ford II, the group helped reorganize Ford Motor Company. McNamara rose steadily and became the first non-family member to serve as the company’s president. When John F. Kennedy was elected president, he offered McNamara his choice of serving as secretary of the treasury or secretary of defense. McNamara chose defense. By 1967, McNamara privately urged President Lyndon Johnson to deescalate, arguing the war was unwinnable. pages.text: Wednesday, January 14, 2026 23 BUSINESS SPOTLIGHT Harmony brings innovative dentistry to downtown Oakland By Allyson Aleksey A new dental practice is taking an unconventional approach to oral health, blending dentistry with medical screening and preventative care while offering a full range of services under one roof in the heart of downtown Oakland. Harmony Whole Person Oral Dental Care, led by longtime dentist and educator Dr. Greg Kaplan, integrates routine dental care with screenings for blood pressure, sleep disorders and chronic conditions, aiming to catch health issues early while Dr. Greg Kaplan M y little p a t i e n t n making care more accessible to East Bay residents. Kaplan said the concept grew out of decades in dentistry and a belief that dental offices can play a larger role in preventive health, particularly for patients who may not regularly see a primary care provider. “About 29 million Americans every year see a dentist and don’t see another health care provider,” Kaplan said. “That creates both a responsibility and an opportunity.” At Harmony, every patient over age 12 receives a blood pressure screening as part of a standard visit. Adults and children are also evaluated for sleep-related issues, including sleep apnea, which research has linked to cardiovascular disease, learning difficulties and behavioral challenges. New patients are offered optional A1C testing, which can help identify diabetes or prediabetes. The screenings are noninvasive and included as part of care. Dr. Kaplan said they have been widely accepted by patients since the practice’s opening in late 2025, and added that they are just as essential to dental health as physical health. In one early case, a patient was referred immediately to urgent care after an elevated blood pressure reading during a dental visit. “[The patient] later called and said her doctor told her she could have had a stroke or heart attack that day,” Kaplan said. The practice’s pediatric focus extends beyond cavities and braces. By evaluating jaw development and facial growth in young children, Kaplan said dentists can help reduce the risk of future sleep disorders and related health problems. e “It’s not just about straight e teeth,” he said. “It’s about how a d child breathes, sleeps and functions.” p a ti e n s Harmony also emphasizes coordination with physicians, particularly when treating sleep apnea through oral appliances or combined therapies. Kaplan said collaboration between dental and medical providers is imperative “if health care systems are to become more preventive and data-driven.” That data-driven approach is central to the practice’s design. Harmony uses an electronic health record system adapted for dentistry, allowing clinicians to track trends such as links between periodontal disease and diabetes while protecting patient privacy. Kaplan said the goal is to better understand how dental and medical care intersect and how c e . that information could improve outcomes over time. “Small steps can lead to big changes,” he said. “If dentists and physicians work together, we can catch problems earlier, improve outcomes and maybe even lower health care costs over time.” Kaplan has been practicing dentistry for decades and taught at the University of Southern California’s dental school for 12 years. Harmony, he said, represents a culmination of those experiences, like a “concept car” for what dentistry could become. “I’m not a young guy just starting out,” he said. “At this point in my career, I wanted to see if we could raise the profession to a new level. Not just great clinical care, but care that’s integrated, transparent and focused on wellness.” The office’s opening comes at a time when many dental practices are moving away from traditional insurance models. Harmony, by contrast, accepts major PPO dental plans and is currently seeking approval to accept Medi-Cal patients, a process Kaplan described as lengthy but necessary. “We want to be available to the community,” he said. “There are a lot of families in the East Bay who need care that’s affordable and accessible.” The downtown Oakland location was chosen intentionally, Kaplan said, despite concerns about post-pandemic foot traffic in downtown centres. He said he believes health care providers play a stabilizing role in city cores and can help support surrounding businesses and community life. “Communities are stronger when people invest in them,” he said. The practice itself was designed to reduce “dental office” anxiety, housed in a bright, fullfloor office space with open spaces, digital check-in options and an emphasis on same-day exams and cleanings when possible. The building is LEED Gold certified, reflecting a commitment to environmental sustainability alongside patient care. Patient response has been largely positive, Kaplan said, with strong online reviews and high participation in optional screenings. As Harmony Whole Person Oral Dental Care settles into its role downtown, Kaplan hopes the practice will not only serve patients, but help reshape how dentistry fits into the broader health care system. “If we can help people live longer, healthier lives by taking a few extra steps,” he said, “that’s a change worth making.” Harmony Whole Person Oral Dental Care is located at 1333 Broadway in Downtown Oakland, third floor. articles.text: Marilyn Farran Clowdsley, born May 6, 1930, passed away peacefully on January 8, 2026. She was the daughter of Dorothy Seawell Farran and Reginald Mansfield Farran and grew up in Piedmont, California, where she spent most of her life. In her later years, Marilyn resided in Rossmoor. articles.text: On a cool, rainy Januar 5 afternoon, 22 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group gathered inside Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. The group met to discuss its December selection, Cry, the Beloved Country by Alan Paton, suggested by Bob Hall. Published in 1948, the same year apartheid was formally instituted in South Africa, the novel follows a Zulu pastor searching for his son in Johannesburg. The son becomes involved in the murder of a white man who was an advocate for racial justice. Set against the backdrop of South Africa just before apartheid became law, the novel is a social protest written by a white South African author. Readers noted that Paton explores themes of love, hope and separation, as well as the devastating effects of racial segregation. The story also examines the breakdown of tribal life, family disintegration, urban poverty, crime and environmental destruction, while still offering the possibility of reconciliation and hope. Sometimes the most challenging discussions arise when everyone likes the book, and that proved to be the case this month. Several readers found the novel easy to read, with one saying she “didn’t want to put it down.” The group praised Paton’s fluid, rhythmic writing style and agreed the book was powerful when it was published and remains so today. Many found the story deeply moving, particularly the parallel grief experienced by the fathers of the murdered man and the young killer. While the losses were heartbreaking, readers also pointed to acts of kindness in the story that felt uplifting. Some members had read the book earlier in life and initially wondered whether it would still resonate. They agreed it remains both wonderful and relevant, though a few felt that little has changed since it was written. Issues such as racial discrimination, crime, environmental damage, immigration struggles and family breakdown still feel painfully familiar. Readers discussed how the young murderer’s actions were shaped by his circumstances. Many felt he was not inherently evil, but a product of his environment, where theft could seem like survival and violence a tragic consequence. Several noted parallels with how some people caught in similar conditions may act today. The group observed that South African politics were largely absent from the novel, which readers felt allowed them to focus more closely on the characters themselves. Even so, many believed the reality of the time was likely harsher than what was depicted. The word “cry” in the book’s title resonated in multiple ways for readers, reflecting sorrow over the deaths of young people, damage to the land, and the African population’s resignation to unbearable conditions. Discussion turned briefly to the present day, with differing views on whether current times are worse than those of the past. While acknowledging real challenges, some readers expressed optimism, noting that progress is rarely linear and that many lives have improved over the past eight decades. Others questioned the novel’s hopeful conclusion, describing it as overly idealistic, but agreed it left much to reflect on. After the discussion, the group December book, Cry, the Beloved County by Alan Paton revisited its use of a handheld microphone to help amplify comments in Community Hall’s large, high-ceilinged space. While passing the microphone around the circle can feel awkward, members agreed it improves accessibility and helps ensure everyone can fully participate in the discussion. The readers had previously selected The Wide Wide Sea: Imperial Ambition, First Contact and the Fateful Final Voyage of Captain James Cook by Hampton Sides for their February read and Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead for their March book. After Phyllis Van Kranenburgh’s presentation of three non-fiction candidates the group selected Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets, a 2013 book by Belarusian Nobel laureate Svetlana Alexievich for April The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion that on February 2 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https://bit.ly/3R86PP4, or call 510 420-3070, to register. Among those participating in the discussion were Mary Carter, Peggy Shultz, Heidi Schmidt, Laura Goldman, Hilary Honore, Lois Price, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Rich Siegel, Orrel Lanter, Bella Almanzan, Phil Witte, Madie Hall, Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Bob Hall, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased Robert White and Odette Pollar were with them for the first time.

After being stolen the vehicle and attached trailer, filled with concrete and dirt from the City’s paving project, crashed into a tree on Ricardo Avenue, coming to rest just feet from a residence’s living room.
